title: Die drei Federn
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 63. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, hieng, Thüre, todt und ward).
about: KHM 63, a Dummling tale in which the youngest son meets his father’s test three times over, is refused the kingdom twice, and has to win it a fourth time. The feather that will not fly far drops him at a trapdoor in the ground, and beneath it a great fat toad gives him carpet and ring out of her box, and a bride out of the circle of little toads sitting round her; the clever brothers, who never trouble to search at all, come back with a shepherd woman’s rags and the hoop off a cart. Grimm’s own gloss of the dialect word Itsche stands in the 1857 text and is kept here, and the spelling is that edition’s, so you will meet gescheidt, Thüre, ausgehölt, hieng and todt.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein König, der hatte drei Söhne, davon waren zwei klug und gescheidt, aber der dritte sprach nicht viel, war einfältig und hieß nur der Dummling.
sentences.l: There was once a king, he had three sons, of them two were clever and shrewd, but the third did not speak much, was simple, and was called only the Dummling.
sentences.i: There was once a king who had three sons. Two of them were clever and quick-witted, but the third said little; he was simple, and they called him nothing but Dummling.
sentences.n: gescheidt is the 1857 spelling of gescheit, clever. einfältig is simple, plain-minded — not stupid outright. Dummling is dumm with the suffix -ling, which makes a person out of a quality: “the simple one.” We leave the nickname in German, as Grimm’s readers heard it.

sentences.t: Als der König alt und schwach ward und an sein Ende dachte, wußte er nicht welcher von seinen Söhnen nach ihm das Reich erben sollte.
sentences.l: When the king became old and weak and thought upon his end, he did not know which of his sons should inherit the kingdom after him.
sentences.n: ward is the 1857 preterite of werden, where modern German writes wurde. “an sein Ende denken” — to think on one’s end, that is, on dying.

sentences.t: Da sprach er zu ihnen „ziehet aus, und wer mir den feinsten Teppich bringt, der soll nach meinem Tod König sein.“
sentences.l: Then he spoke to them “go forth, and whoever brings me the finest carpet, he shall be king after my death.”
sentences.i: Then he said to them: “Go out into the world, and whoever brings me the finest carpet shall be king after my death.”
sentences.n: ziehet is the old full imperative plural, modern zieht. ausziehen here is to set out on one’s travels.

sentences.t: Und damit es keinen Streit unter ihnen gab, führte er sie vor sein Schloß, blies drei Federn in die Luft und sprach „wie die fliegen, so sollt ihr ziehen.“
sentences.l: And so that there should be no quarrel among them, he led them out before his castle, blew three feathers into the air and spoke “as these fly, so shall you go.”
sentences.i: And so that there should be no quarrel among them, he led them out in front of his castle, blew three feathers into the air, and said: “As these fly, so shall you travel.”
sentences.n: damit opens a purpose clause, so that. In “wie die fliegen, so sollt ihr ziehen,” die is a demonstrative pointing back at the feathers, not a relative pronoun.

sentences.t: Die eine Feder flog nach Osten, die andere nach Westen, die dritte flog aber gerad aus, und flog nicht weit, sondern fiel bald zur Erde.
sentences.l: The one feather flew toward the east, the other toward the west, but the third flew straight ahead, and flew not far, but rather soon fell to the earth.
sentences.i: One feather flew east, the other west; but the third flew straight ahead, and did not fly far — it soon fell to the ground.
sentences.n: gerad aus is modern geradeaus, straight ahead, still written as two words here.

sentences.t: Nun gieng der eine Bruder rechts, der andere gieng links, und sie lachten den Dummling aus, der bei der dritten Feder da wo sie nieder gefallen war, bleiben mußte.
sentences.l: Now the one brother went right, the other went left, and they laughed the Dummling out, who had to stay by the third feather, there where it had fallen down.
sentences.i: So one brother went to the right and the other to the left, and they mocked Dummling, who had to stay by the third feather, on the spot where it had fallen.
sentences.n: auslachen is to laugh at, to jeer — the particle aus is what makes the laughter derisive; here it stands at the end, “lachten… aus.”

sentences.t: Der Dummling setzte sich nieder und war traurig.
sentences.l: The Dummling set himself down and was sad.
sentences.i: Dummling sat down and was sad.

sentences.t: Da bemerkte er auf einmal daß neben der Feder eine Fallthüre lag.
sentences.l: Then he noticed all at once that beside the feather a trap-door lay.
sentences.i: Then all at once he noticed that a trapdoor lay beside the feather.
sentences.n: Fallthüre is modern Falltür, a trapdoor — a Thür that you fall through.

sentences.t: Er hob sie in die Höhe, fand eine Treppe und stieg hinab.
sentences.l: He lifted it up into the height, found a stair and climbed down.
sentences.i: He raised it, found a stairway, and climbed down.

sentences.t: Da kam er vor eine andere Thüre, klopfte an, und hörte wie es inwendig rief
sentences.l: There he came before another door, knocked, and heard how inside it called
sentences.i: There he came to another door, knocked, and heard something calling within:
sentences.n: inwendig is the old word for inside, where modern German says drinnen. The line has no full stop: the verse completes it.

sentences.t:
„Jungfer grün und klein,
Hutzelbein,
Hutzelbeins Hündchen,
Hutzel hin und her,
laß geschwind sehen, wer draußen wär.“
sentences.l:
“Maiden green and small,
Shrivel-shank,
Shrivel-shank’s little dog,
Shrivel here and there,
let [us] see quickly, who might be outside.”
sentences.i:
“Green little maiden,
Shrivel-shank,
Shrivel-shank’s little dog,
shrivel to and fro —
let us see quickly who is outside.”
sentences.n: A summoning rhyme, and mostly nonsense on purpose. Hutzel is a shrivelled, dried thing — a dried pear, above all — so Hutzelbein is something like “shrivel-leg,” and that is how we render it; but what the name is meant to denote here is genuinely uncertain, and the rhyme may be nearer nonsense than sense. “laß geschwind sehen” leaves out the object: let [us] see quickly. wär is the subjunctive of a thing not yet known.

sentences.t: Die Thüre that sich auf, und er sah eine große dicke Itsche (Kröte) sitzen und rings um sie eine Menge kleiner Itschen.
sentences.l: The door did itself open, and he saw a great fat Itsche (toad) sitting, and round about her a crowd of little Itschen.
sentences.i: The door opened, and he saw a great fat toad sitting there, with a host of little toads all around her.
sentences.n: “sich aufthun” = to open, of a door that opens by itself; that is the archaic spelling of tat, from thun = modern tun. Itsche is a dialect word for a toad, and Grimm supplies the standard Kröte in parentheses in the 1857 text itself — his gloss, which we keep.

sentences.t: Die dicke Itsche fragte was sein Begehren wäre.
sentences.l: The fat Itsche asked what his desire might be.
sentences.i: The fat toad asked what he wanted.
sentences.n: Begehren is the verb begehren (to desire) used as a noun: his request, what he was after.

sentences.t: Er antwortete „ich hätte gerne den schönsten und feinsten Teppich.“
sentences.l: He answered “I would gladly have the most beautiful and finest carpet.”
sentences.i: He answered: “I should like to have the most beautiful and finest carpet.”
sentences.n: “ich hätte gerne” — a conditional used for politeness, and still the ordinary German way of asking for a thing.

sentences.t: Da rief sie eine junge und sprach
sentences.l: Then she called a young one and spoke
sentences.i: Then she called a young one and said:
sentences.n: “eine junge” — the adjective stands alone as a noun: a young [toad]. No full stop again; the verse finishes the sentence.

sentences.t:
„Jungfer grün und klein,
Hutzelbein,
Hutzelbeins Hündchen,
Hutzel hin und her,
bring mir die große Schachtel her.“
sentences.l:
“Maiden green and small,
Shrivel-shank,
Shrivel-shank’s little dog,
Shrivel here and there,
bring me the great box here.”
sentences.i:
“Green little maiden,
Shrivel-shank,
Shrivel-shank’s little dog,
shrivel to and fro —
bring me the great box here.”
sentences.n: The same rhyme with the last line exchanged: the formula is the household’s bell, and only the errand changes.

sentences.t: Die junge Itsche holte die Schachtel, und die dicke Itsche machte sie auf und gab dem Dummling einen Teppich daraus, so schön und so fein, wie oben auf der Erde keiner konnte gewebt werden.
sentences.l: The young Itsche fetched the box, and the fat Itsche opened it up and gave the Dummling a carpet out of it, so beautiful and so fine as none could be woven up above on the earth.
sentences.i: The young toad fetched the box, and the fat toad opened it and gave Dummling a carpet out of it, so beautiful and so fine that none like it could be woven up above on the earth.
sentences.n: “oben auf der Erde” — up on the earth, that is, in the world above; the toads’ realm is under it, which is why the carpet is beyond any weaver’s reach.

sentences.t: Da dankte er ihr und stieg wieder hinauf.
sentences.l: Then he thanked her and climbed up again.

sentences.t: Die beiden andern hatten aber ihren jüngsten Bruder für so albern gehalten, daß sie glaubten er würde gar nichts finden und aufbringen.
sentences.l: But the two others had held their youngest brother for so silly that they believed he would find and bring up nothing at all.
sentences.i: But the two others had taken their youngest brother for such a fool that they were sure he would find nothing at all and produce nothing.
sentences.n: “halten für” = to take someone for, to reckon him as. aufbringen here is to bring up, to come up with something to show.

sentences.t: „Was sollen wir uns mit Suchen groß Mühe geben“ sprachen sie, nahmen dem ersten besten Schäfersweib, das ihnen begegnete, die groben Tücher vom Leib und trugen sie dem König heim.
sentences.l: “Why should we give ourselves great trouble with searching,” they spoke, took from the first shepherd’s-wife that met them the coarse cloths off her body and carried them home to the king.
sentences.i: “Why should we put ourselves to any great trouble with searching?” they said, and took the coarse cloths off the back of the first shepherd’s wife they met, and carried them home to the king.
sentences.n: “sich Mühe geben” = to take pains. “der erste beste” is a fixed phrase: the first that comes along, whoever it happens to be. In “nahmen dem Schäfersweib… die Tücher vom Leib” the woman stands in the dative — they took the cloths from her, off her body, and she is given no say in it.

sentences.t: Zu derselben Zeit kam auch der Dummling zurück, und brachte seinen schönen Teppich, und als der König den sah, erstaunte er, und sprach „wenn es dem Recht nach gehen soll, so gehört dem jüngsten das Königreich.“
sentences.l: At the same time the Dummling also came back, and brought his beautiful carpet, and when the king saw it, he was astonished, and spoke “if it is to go according to right, then the kingdom belongs to the youngest.”
sentences.i: At the same time Dummling came back too and brought his beautiful carpet; and when the king saw it he was astonished, and said: “If the thing is to go by right, then the kingdom belongs to the youngest.”
sentences.n: “dem Recht nach” = according to what is just; nach follows its noun here. gehören takes the dative: the kingdom belongs to him.

sentences.t: Aber die zwei andern ließen dem Vater keine Ruhe und sprachen unmöglich könnte der Dummling, dem es in allen Dingen an Verstand fehlte, König werden, und baten ihn er möchte eine neue Bedingung machen.
sentences.l: But the two others let the father have no peace and said the Dummling, who lacked understanding in all things, could not possibly become king, and begged him he might make a new condition.
sentences.i: But the two others gave their father no peace, and said that Dummling, who wanted sense in everything, could not possibly become king; and they begged him to set a new condition.
sentences.n: “es fehlt ihm an etwas” is impersonal — es is the subject, the person stands in the dative (dem), and the thing lacked follows an: he is short of understanding.

sentences.t: Da sagte der Vater, „der soll das Reich erben, der mir den schönsten Ring bringt,“ führte die drei Brüder hinaus, und blies drei Federn in die Luft, denen sie nachgehen sollten.
sentences.l: Then the father said, “he shall inherit the kingdom, who brings me the most beautiful ring,” led the three brothers out, and blew three feathers into the air, which they were to follow.
sentences.i: Then the father said: “He shall inherit the kingdom who brings me the most beautiful ring” — and he led the three brothers out and blew three feathers into the air for them to follow.
sentences.n: “der… der…” — the first der points ahead (“that one”), the second opens the relative clause. nachgehen takes the dative, hence denen.

sentences.t: Die zwei ältesten zogen wieder nach Osten und Westen, und für den Dummling flog die Feder gerade aus und fiel neben der Erdthüre nieder.
sentences.l: The two eldest went again toward east and west, and for the Dummling the feather flew straight ahead and fell down beside the earth-door.
sentences.i: The two eldest went off east and west again, and for Dummling the feather flew straight ahead and fell beside the door in the earth.
sentences.n: Erdthüre is a compound the tale coins on the spot for the trapdoor in the ground — Erde plus Thüre.

sentences.t: Da stieg er wieder hinab zu der dicken Itsche und sagte ihr daß er den schönsten Ring brauchte.
sentences.l: Then he climbed down again to the fat Itsche and told her that he needed the most beautiful ring.

sentences.t: Sie ließ sich gleich ihre große Schachtel holen und gab ihm daraus einen Ring, der glänzte von Edelsteinen und war so schön daß ihn kein Goldschmied auf der Erde hätte machen können.
sentences.l: She had her great box fetched at once and gave him a ring out of it, which shone with jewels and was so beautiful that no goldsmith on the earth could have made it.
sentences.i: She had her great box brought at once and gave him a ring out of it that shone with precious stones, and was so beautiful that no goldsmith on earth could have made it.
sentences.n: “sich etwas holen lassen” is causative: she has it fetched for her rather than fetching it. “hätte machen können” is the past subjunctive of a thing that could not have happened.

sentences.t: Die zwei ältesten lachten über den Dummling, der einen goldenen Ring suchen wollte, gaben sich gar keine Mühe, sondern schlugen einem alten Wagenring die Nägel aus und brachten ihn dem König.
sentences.l: The two eldest laughed over the Dummling, who wanted to look for a golden ring, gave themselves no trouble at all, but rather knocked the nails out of an old cart-ring and brought it to the king.
sentences.i: The two eldest laughed at Dummling for wanting to look for a golden ring; they took no trouble at all, but knocked the nails out of an old cart-hoop and brought that to the king.
sentences.n: A Wagenring is an iron hoop belonging to a cart — the band shrunk and nailed onto a wheel; knocking out its nails is the whole of their labour. ausschlagen stands split: “schlugen… aus.”

sentences.t: Als aber der Dummling seinen goldenen Ring vorzeigte, so sprach der Vater abermals „ihm gehört das Reich.“
sentences.l: But when the Dummling showed his golden ring, then the father spoke once again “to him belongs the kingdom.”
sentences.i: But when Dummling produced his golden ring, the father said once again: “The kingdom belongs to him.”
sentences.n: vorzeigen is to show, to produce for inspection. abermals is an old-fashioned “once again,” kept for solemn repetitions.

sentences.t: Die zwei ältesten ließen nicht ab den König zu quälen, bis er noch eine dritte Bedingung machte und den Ausspruch that, der sollte das Reich haben, der die schönste Frau heimbrächte.
sentences.l: The two eldest did not leave off tormenting the king, until he made yet a third condition and gave the pronouncement, he should have the kingdom who brought the most beautiful wife home.
sentences.i: The two eldest did not leave off plaguing the king until he made yet a third condition and gave out the ruling: he should have the kingdom who brought home the most beautiful wife.
sentences.n: ablassen = to leave off, separable: “ließen… ab.” “den Ausspruch thun” = to deliver the pronouncement (that is thun = modern tun). heimbrächte is the subjunctive of reported speech, carrying the king’s words.

sentences.t: Die drei Federn blies er nochmals in die Luft, und sie flogen wie die vorigemale.
sentences.l: The three feathers he blew once more into the air, and they flew as the previous times.
sentences.i: He blew the three feathers into the air once more, and they flew as they had the times before.
sentences.n: “die vorigemale” = the previous times, written as one word here; modern German has die vorigen Male.

sentences.t: Da gieng der Dummling ohne weiteres hinab zu der dicken Itsche und sprach „ich soll die schönste Frau heimbringen.“
sentences.l: Then the Dummling went down without further ado to the fat Itsche and spoke “I am to bring home the most beautiful wife.”
sentences.i: So Dummling went straight down to the fat toad and said: “I am to bring home the most beautiful wife.”
sentences.n: “ohne weiteres” = without more ado, without stopping to think about it. By the third errand he no longer knocks or waits.

sentences.t: „Ei,“ antwortete die Itsche, „die schönste Frau! die ist nicht gleich zur Hand, aber du sollst sie doch haben.“
sentences.l: “Well now,” answered the Itsche, “the most beautiful wife! she is not right to hand, but you shall have her nevertheless.”
sentences.i: “Well!” answered the toad. “The most beautiful wife! She is not to be had at a moment’s notice — but you shall have her all the same.”
sentences.n: “zur Hand” = to hand, ready at once. doch here is the concessive “all the same.”

sentences.t: Sie gab ihm eine ausgehölte gelbe Rübe mit sechs Mäuschen bespannt.
sentences.l: She gave him a hollowed-out yellow root harnessed with six little mice.
sentences.i: She gave him a hollowed-out yellow root with six little mice harnessed to it.
sentences.n: ausgehölt is the 1857 spelling of ausgehöhlt, hollowed out. “gelbe Rübe” is a yellow root vegetable: in the south the phrase means a carrot, elsewhere a yellow turnip, and which is meant here cannot be settled from the text. bespannt is the proper word for a team harnessed to a vehicle — the root is already a carriage before anyone says so.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Dummling ganz traurig „was soll ich damit anfangen?“
sentences.l: Then the Dummling spoke quite sadly “what shall I begin with that?”
sentences.i: Then Dummling said quite sadly: “What am I to do with that?”
sentences.n: “was soll ich damit anfangen” is fixed: literally “what am I to begin with it,” meaning what use is it to me.

sentences.t: Die Itsche antwortete „setze nur eine von meinen kleinen Itschen hinein.“
sentences.l: The Itsche answered “just set one of my little Itschen inside.”
sentences.i: The toad answered: “Only set one of my little toads inside.”

sentences.t: Da griff er auf Gerathewohl eine aus dem Kreiß und setzte sie in die gelbe Kutsche, aber kaum saß sie darin, so ward sie zu einem wunderschönen Fräulein, die Rübe zur Kutsche, und die sechs Mäuschen zu Pferden.
sentences.l: Then he seized one at random out of the circle and set her in the yellow coach, but scarcely was she sitting in it when she became a wondrously beautiful young lady, the root a coach, and the six little mice horses.
sentences.i: So he took one at random out of the ring and set her in the yellow coach; but scarcely was she inside when she turned into a wondrously beautiful young lady, the root into a coach, and the six little mice into horses.
sentences.n: “auf Gerathewohl” = at random, on the off-chance; modern aufs Geratewohl. Kreiß is the 1857 spelling of Kreis, here the ring of little toads sitting round the big one. “werden zu” = to turn into.

sentences.t: Da küßte er sie, jagte mit den Pferden davon und brachte sie zu dem König.
sentences.l: Then he kissed her, drove off with the horses and brought her to the king.
sentences.i: Then he kissed her, drove away at a gallop, and brought her to the king.
sentences.n: jagen here is to drive at speed, not to hunt.

sentences.t: Seine Brüder kamen nach, die hatten sich gar keine Mühe gegeben, eine schöne Frau zu suchen, sondern die ersten besten Bauernweiber mitgenommen.
sentences.l: His brothers came after; they had given themselves no trouble at all to look for a beautiful wife, but rather had taken along the first peasant-women that came.
sentences.i: His brothers came along behind; they had taken no trouble at all to look for a beautiful wife, but had simply brought the first peasant women that came to hand.
sentences.n: “die ersten besten” again — whoever happens to be nearest. The brothers’ method never changes; only what they seize does.

sentences.t: Als der König sie erblickte, sprach er „dem jüngsten gehört das Reich nach meinem Tod.“
sentences.l: When the king caught sight of her, he spoke “to the youngest belongs the kingdom after my death.”
sentences.i: When the king caught sight of her, he said: “The kingdom belongs to the youngest after my death.”

sentences.t: Aber die zwei ältesten betäubten die Ohren des Königs aufs neue mit ihrem Geschrei, „wir könnens nicht zugeben daß der Dummling König wird,“ und verlangten der sollte den Vorzug haben, dessen Frau durch einen Ring springen könnte, der da mitten in dem Saal hieng.
sentences.l: But the two eldest deafened the ears of the king anew with their shouting, “we cannot allow it that the Dummling becomes king,” and demanded that he should have the preference, whose wife could spring through a ring that hung there in the middle of the hall.
sentences.i: But the two eldest deafened the king’s ears afresh with their clamour — “We cannot allow Dummling to become king!” — and demanded that the preference go to the one whose wife could leap through a ring that hung there in the middle of the hall.
sentences.n: betäuben is to stun, to deafen; “aufs neue” = anew. könnens = können es. zugeben here means to permit, not to admit. dessen is the genitive relative: the man whose wife. hieng = hing, the archaic -ie-.

sentences.t: Sie dachten „die Bauernweiber können das wohl, die sind stark genug, aber das zarte Fräulein springt sich todt.“
sentences.l: They thought “the peasant-women can do that well enough, they are strong enough, but the delicate young lady will spring herself dead.”
sentences.i: They thought: “The peasant women can manage that well enough — they are strong; but the delicate young lady will leap herself to death.”
sentences.n: “sich todt springen” — a reflexive with an adjective naming the outcome of the action: to leap oneself dead. The brothers are not proposing a contest; they are proposing a death.

sentences.t: Der alte König gab das auch noch zu.
sentences.l: The old king allowed that too.
sentences.i: The old king granted them that as well.
sentences.n: He has now been talked out of his own judgment for the third time, and in a single line each time.

sentences.t: Da sprangen die zwei Bauernweiber, sprangen auch durch den Ring, waren aber so plump, daß sie fielen und ihre groben Arme und Beine entzwei brachen.
sentences.l: Then the two peasant-women sprang, sprang through the ring too, but were so clumsy that they fell and broke their coarse arms and legs in two.
sentences.i: So the two peasant women leapt, and did get through the ring; but they were so heavy and clumsy that they fell and broke their thick arms and legs in two.
sentences.n: plump is heavy, thick-set, clumsy. entzwei = in two, apart. Nothing is softened and nothing is said afterwards about the two of them.

sentences.t: Darauf sprang das schöne Fräulein, das der Dummling mitgebracht hatte, und sprang so leicht hindurch wie ein Reh, und aller Widerspruch mußte aufhören.
sentences.l: Thereupon sprang the beautiful young lady, whom the Dummling had brought along, and sprang through as lightly as a roe, and all objection had to cease.
sentences.i: Then the beautiful young lady whom Dummling had brought sprang, and went through as lightly as a roe deer, and all objection had to end.
sentences.n: Ein Reh is the small European roe deer, the standard figure for lightness in German as a fawn is in English.

sentences.t: Also erhielt er die Krone, und hat lange in Weisheit geherrscht.
sentences.l: So he received the crown, and has ruled long in wisdom.
sentences.i: And so he received the crown, and ruled long and wisely.
sentences.n: also here is the old “thus, and so,” not the modern “also.” The closing verb is a perfect — “hat… geherrscht” — which quietly puts the teller in a present looking back on it.
